Rosh Hashanah. The Jewish New Year falls on the first and second days of Tishrei, in September or October. It opens the High Holy Days, a ten-day period of introspection and repentance that culminates in Yom Kippur, and commemorates God's creation of the world. It is celebrated as a day of judgment when one's actions of the past year are weighed.

The shofar, a ram's horn, is blown throughout the holiday to call people to spiritual awakening and repentance. Apples dipped in honey are eaten as a symbol of hope for a sweet new year. The talit, or prayer shawl, is worn during morning prayers as a sign of respect and solemnity. The holiday lasts two days, making it one of the longer Jewish holidays in observance.

The New Year date itself, the first of Tishrei, is not mentioned explicitly in the Torah; the tradition developed through rabbinic interpretation. Congregational prayers include the Unetaneh Tokef, a powerful liturgical poem about divine judgment. The traditional greeting is L'shana tova, which means "for a good year," to wish others well in the coming year. The holiday is deeply connected to the concept of teshuvah, repentance and return, beginning a season of self-examination that opens the period of judgment and repentance completed by Yom Kippur.
